course.title: Darwin's Natural Selection: Reading Chapter IV of On the Origin of Species
course.description: A close reading of the opening of Chapter IV of Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859), in which he defines natural selection and previews the arguments that follow. The course grounds every lesson in Darwin's own words, working from the chapter's summary heading through his step-by-step reasoning from variation and heredity to the preservation of favourable variations.

lessons.title: The Chapter's Argument in Miniature
lessons.content:
# The Chapter's Argument in Miniature

## A heading that is really an outline

Victorian scientific books often opened each chapter with a dense, telegraphic summary — a string of phrases separated by commas and full stops, listing the topics in the order they appear. Modern readers skim past these. Don't. Darwin's heading to Chapter IV is the whole argument compressed into about eighty words, and if you unfold it carefully you already know where the chapter is going and why the parts are in that order.

Here it is:

> Natural Selection: its power compared with man's selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes. Sexual Selection. On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species. Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals. Slow action. Extinction caused by Natural Selection. Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation. Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent. Explains the Grouping of all organic beings.

Notice the shape. It begins with a **comparison** (nature versus the breeder), passes through **scope** claims (what kinds of characters, which ages, which sexes), then **qualifications and conditions** (intercrossing, isolation, numbers, slowness), then **consequences** (extinction, divergence), and ends with a single triumphant **explanatory payoff**: the grouping of all organic beings. That is the structure of an argument, not a list of topics.

## Unfolding the clauses

**"Its power compared with man's selection."** Chapter I of the *Origin* was about domestic pigeons, dogs, cabbages — variation under domestication. Darwin has already shown that the breeder, by picking which individuals reproduce, can remake a species. Chapter IV's opening move is to ask whether nature can do the same thing. The comparison is a rhetorical bridge from the familiar to the contested: *you already believe in selection; I am only asking who is doing the selecting.*

**"Its power on characters of trifling importance."** Man selects what he can see and what he cares about — plumage colour, size of fruit. Nature, Darwin will argue, scrutinises everything, including features so small that no human observer would notice them. This clause pre-empts the objection that natural selection could only handle large, obvious organs.

**"Its power at all ages and on both sexes."** Selection is not restricted to adults. A variation that helps a larva, a seedling, or a nestling is just as preservable as one that helps a breeding adult. And it can act differently on males and females — which is why the very next words of the heading are "Sexual Selection."

**"Circumstances favourable and unfavourable... Slow action."** Darwin builds his own objections into the outline. Intercrossing can blend away a novelty; small populations offer fewer variations; the process is glacially slow. A weaker author would bury these; Darwin advertises them.

**"Explains the Grouping of all organic beings."** This is the prize. The final clause claims that natural selection, working through divergence and extinction on the descendants of a common parent, accounts for why life falls into nested groups — species within genera within families — the very pattern that taxonomists had been describing for a century without explaining.

## The argument delivered, in one paragraph

The chapter's first paragraph is the heading's first clause cashed out. Strip it to its bones and you get a chain of premises:

1. Organisms vary — endlessly and strangely under domestication, less so but really in nature.
2. Variation is heritable: "how strong the hereditary tendency is."
3. The relations of organisms to each other and to their conditions are "infinitely complex and close-fitting" — so there are countless ways a slight change could matter.
4. Since variations useful *to man* demonstrably occur, variations useful *to the organism* must sometimes occur too, over thousands of generations.
5. Many more individuals are born than can survive (the struggle for existence, from Chapter III).
6. Therefore individuals with "any advantage, however slight" have the best chance of surviving and reproducing; and "any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed."

And then the definition, which is a *name* given to the conclusion rather than a new assumption:

> "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection."

Note what the term is defined as: a two-sided process, preservation *and* rejection. It is not a force added to the world; it is the bookkeeping consequence of premises 1–5.

## The clause most readers skip

Darwin immediately adds a limit:

> "Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic."

This is a striking piece of intellectual honesty and, in hindsight, a remarkable anticipation. Selection has *no grip* on neutral variation. Such traits drift, fluctuate, and may persist in several forms at once — which Darwin suggests might explain polymorphic species, those in which several distinct forms coexist without any one prevailing. Twentieth-century population genetics would make this the theory of neutral evolution; Darwin gets it as a one-sentence caveat.

It also tells you something about how to read him. Darwin does not claim selection explains every feature of every organism. He claims it explains *useful* features — and says so in the same breath as the definition.

## How to use the heading as a reading tool

A practical exercise: copy the heading onto a card. As you work through Chapter IV, tick each clause off when you find the passage that discharges it. You will find that Darwin does them almost strictly in order, and that the ones he spends longest on (divergence of character, the conditions favouring selection) are the ones he expected to be doubted. The length of treatment is a map of nineteenth-century resistance.

**Question to hold onto:** the heading promises that natural selection "Explains the Grouping of all organic beings." Before reading further, ask yourself what would need to be true for descent, divergence, and extinction to produce a *branching, nested* pattern rather than, say, a smooth continuum of forms. Darwin's answer is the destination of the chapter.

lessons.title: The Topics Darwin Promises to Cover
lessons.content:
# The Topics Darwin Promises to Cover

Victorian books often opened each chapter with a dense "argument" or heading — a telegraphic list of the contents, printed as a single paragraph. These headings are easy to skim past, but Darwin's is worth reading as a table of contents *and* as a map of an argument. It tells you not only what he will discuss but the order in which the pieces must be assembled.

Here is the heading of Chapter IV in full:

> Natural Selection: its power compared with man's selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes. Sexual Selection. On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species. Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals. Slow action. Extinction caused by Natural Selection. Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation. Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent. Explains the Grouping of all organic beings.

This lesson surveys the topics announced after the opening clauses — sexual selection, intercrossing, the favourable and unfavourable circumstances, slow action, extinction, and divergence of character — and shows how they hang together.

---

## The shape of the chapter

Before taking the topics one at a time, notice the overall movement. The heading proceeds in four stages:

1. **The mechanism and its reach.** Natural selection compared with man's selection; its power on trifling characters; its power at all ages and on both sexes; and then sexual selection as a special case.
2. **A necessary factual premise.** The generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species.
3. **The conditions and tempo of its operation.** Circumstances favourable and unfavourable — intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals — and slow action.
4. **The consequences.** Extinction, divergence of character, and finally the grouping of all organic beings under a common parent.

The argument runs: *here is the engine; here is the medium it runs in; here is when it runs well and how fast; here is what it produces.* Each stage depends on the one before.

---

## Sexual selection

Darwin has just claimed that natural selection acts "at all ages and on both sexes." Sexual selection is the natural next entry, because it explains a class of characters that plain survival-selection struggles with: the stag's antlers, the peacock's train, the cock's spur, the song and colour of male birds. These do not obviously help their bearer survive; some plainly hinder it.

Sexual selection, Darwin says, "depends not on a struggle for existence, but on a struggle between the males for possession of the females; the result is not death to the unsuccessful competitor, but few or no offspring." The currency is the same — differential reproduction — but the arena is different. Placing this topic immediately after "power at all ages and on both sexes" is not accidental: it is a demonstration that selection is subtler than a simple contest for food and safety, and that it can reach characters an unsympathetic critic would call useless.

## The generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species

This is the most technical item in the list and the easiest to underestimate. Darwin devotes real effort to arguing that even hermaphrodite plants and animals occasionally cross with another individual — that self-fertilisation for perpetuity is rare or unknown.

Why does this matter to a theory of natural selection? Two reasons.

- **It supplies the raw variability.** Crossing between individuals keeps stirring the pot, giving selection fresh combinations to act on.
- **It sets up the next topic.** If intercrossing is universal, then the free blending of a whole population is a background fact — and that fact will turn out to be one of the main *obstacles* to selection producing distinct new forms.

So the topic functions as a hinge: it is a positive claim about nature that immediately becomes a constraint in the section that follows.

## Circumstances favourable and unfavourable: intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals

Darwin lists three factors, and they interact.

- **Intercrossing** cuts both ways. It maintains vigour and uniformity within a species, but it also swamps a novel favourable variation by blending it back into the general population.
- **Isolation** counteracts that swamping. A geographically separated group is protected from immigration and free crossing, so a new variety can be slowly perfected. But isolation also limits the number of individuals and the diversity of conditions, so it is not an unmixed good.
- **Number of individuals** favours selection simply because more births mean more variations appearing in a given time. A large area supporting a large population, if it undergoes slow oscillations of level, is Darwin's ideal theatre for producing new and dominant forms.

The honesty here is characteristic: this is a section on what makes his own mechanism *fail*, placed in the middle of the chapter that establishes it.

## Slow action

Having described the conditions, Darwin insists on the timescale. Natural selection "acts only by the preservation and accumulation of infinitesimally small inherited modifications"; it can act only when places in the economy of nature can be better filled, and such openings depend on slow physical or biological change. The topic is a plea for deep time, and it answers an obvious objection — *we do not see this happening* — by replying that we could not possibly see it in a human lifetime.

Slow action also links the conditions to the consequences: extinction and divergence are cumulative outcomes, and they require the long stretches of time this section argues for.

## Extinction caused by natural selection

Extinction is not an accident befalling species from outside; on Darwin's account it is the shadow side of selection itself. Since the number of forms an area supports is limited, the improvement and increase of one form entails the rarity and eventual disappearance of the forms it competes with — and competition is fiercest between the most closely allied forms, varieties of the same species and species of the same genus.

This is why extinction must be discussed *before* divergence and grouping. Selection alone would fill the world with a graded continuum of intermediates; it is extinction that removes the intermediate links and leaves distinct, separated groups behind.

## Divergence of character

This is the keystone topic and Darwin's proudest addition to the argument. The principle: the more diversified the descendants of any one species become, the more different places in the economy of nature they can seize, and so the more of them can live. A plot of ground yields more herbage if sown with several distinct genera of grasses than with one species; a carnivorous quadruped stocked beyond its area's capacity can increase only by its varying descendants taking to new prey, new habitats, new habits.

The heading ties divergence to two lines of evidence:

- **the diversity of inhabitants of any small area** — a patch of turf or a small pond contains species from many genera and orders, which is what one expects if diversity itself confers advantage;
- **naturalisation** — introduced plants and animals that succeed in a new country tend to belong to genera *not* already represented there, again suggesting that unlikeness is what wins a foothold.

## How the pieces combine

The last two clauses of the heading show the synthesis: "Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent. Explains the Grouping of all organic beings."

Divergence and extinction are a pair. Divergence generates the branches; extinction prunes away the trunk and the intermediate twigs. What remains is a set of well-marked groups nested within larger groups — genera within families, families within orders — which is exactly the pattern naturalists had long recorded in classification without being able to explain it. The chapter therefore ends by cashing in every earlier topic: the mechanism, its scope, its medium, its conditions, its pace, and its two great consequences, all deployed to account for the shape of the tree of life.

---

## Reading the heading as a plan

A useful exercise: try re-ordering the topics. Could extinction come before the section on favourable circumstances? Could divergence precede intercrossing? In each case the argument weakens, because Darwin has arranged the list so that every item either supplies a premise for a later one or removes an objection to it. The heading is not a summary written after the fact; it is the architecture of the chapter made visible.

A short reference table:

| Topic | Role in the argument |
|---|---|
| Sexual selection | Extends selection's reach to characters survival cannot explain |
| Generality of intercrosses | Factual premise; also the source of the swamping problem |
| Favourable/unfavourable circumstances | When selection works well, and when it is defeated |
| Slow action | Establishes the timescale the consequences require |
| Extinction | Removes intermediates; the cost of one form's success |
| Divergence of character | Diversity itself is advantageous; generates branches |
| Grouping of organic beings | The synthesis the whole chapter is aimed at |

# Darwin's Opening Question

## Two questions, one hinge

Chapter IV of *On the Origin of Species* opens not with a claim but with a pair of questions:

> "How will the struggle for existence, discussed too briefly in the last chapter, act in regard to variation? Can the principle of selection, which we have seen is so potent in the hands of man, apply in nature?"

Everything that follows in the chapter — the whole machinery of natural selection, divergence of character, extinction, the tree of life — hangs on these two sentences. It is worth slowing down to see exactly what work they are doing.

**Question 1** joins two things Darwin has already established separately in earlier chapters:

- *Variation* (Chapters I–II): organisms differ from one another, in domestication endlessly, and in nature too.
- *The struggle for existence* (Chapter III): more individuals are born than can possibly survive.

Neither of these was controversial on its own. Breeders knew about variation; Malthusian arithmetic about population was familiar. Darwin's question is what happens *when you put them together* — when the struggle operates on a population that is not uniform. The word "how" is important: he is not asking whether the struggle acts on variation, but by what mechanism, with what result.

**Question 2** is the rhetorical hinge. Darwin's readers already accepted that selection works: pigeon fanciers, sheep breeders, and horticulturalists had reshaped domestic species within living memory. That was not speculation; it was an agricultural fact you could buy at a market. So Darwin does not ask his reader to accept a new principle. He asks whether a principle the reader *already accepts* can operate without a human selector.

## The strategy: extension, not invention

This is Darwin's characteristic argumentative move, and it recurs throughout the book. Rather than introducing a novel force, he takes a familiar, uncontested cause and asks how far its reach extends. The burden of proof shifts: the skeptic must now explain why selection should stop at the garden wall.

Notice how the paragraph is built as a chain of "let it be borne in mind" reminders, each one already granted:

1. Domestic productions vary in "an endless number of strange peculiarities," and wild ones vary too, "in a lesser degree."
2. "How strong the hereditary tendency is" — variations are passed on.
3. Under domestication "the whole organisation becomes in some degree plastic."
4. The "mutual relations of all organic beings to each other and to their physical conditions of life" are "infinitely complex and close-fitting."

Then the pivot, framed again as a question rather than an assertion:

> "Can it, then, be thought improbable, seeing that variations useful to man have undoubtedly occurred, that other variations useful in some way to each being in the great and complex battle of life, should sometimes occur in the course of thousands of generations?"

The argument here is *probabilistic*, not deductive. Darwin does not claim to have observed a useful wild variation arise. He argues that given (a) variation demonstrably occurs and is sometimes useful to *human* purposes, and (b) relations among organisms are exquisitely fine-grained, and (c) there are thousands of generations to work with, it would be strange to insist that no variation is ever useful to the organism itself.

Point (4) — close-fitting relations — is doing quiet but heavy lifting. If organisms lived in loose, forgiving circumstances, a slight variation would make no difference. Because the fit between an organism and its world is tight, small differences can matter.

## The conclusion, delivered as a rhetorical question

> "If such do occur, can we doubt (remembering that many more individuals are born than can possibly survive) that individuals having any advantage, however slight, over others, would have the best chance of surviving and of procreating their kind?"

Here the parenthesis carries the argument. The struggle for existence is what converts a *difference* into a *consequence*. Without superabundant birth and inevitable death, an advantage would have no edge to bite on; everyone would survive and the variation would simply accumulate as noise. The parenthesis is the engine, tucked into a subordinate clause.

The symmetrical half follows immediately, and it is the one sentence in the passage stated flatly rather than as a question: "any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed."

## The definition

> "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection."

Note what the definition *is*: a name for a two-sided outcome — preservation plus rejection. It is not a force, not an agent, not a striving. Darwin names a result of the interaction between variation and the struggle for existence.

And note the crucial third case he adds at once:

> "Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic."

This is a striking piece of intellectual honesty. Darwin's mechanism has *limits*, and he states them in the same breath as the mechanism itself. Neutral variation is left to fluctuate — a remark that anticipates, more than a century early, the modern idea of neutral variation and genetic drift. A theorist trying to oversell would have claimed selection explains everything; Darwin explicitly carves out what it does not touch.

## Why the questions matter

Reading the opening as mere rhetorical decoration misses the point. The question form does three things:

- It positions the reader as a judge rather than a convert.
- It makes each premise separately checkable, so a reader who accepts all four "bear in mind" points finds the conclusion already half-built.
- It keeps the claim modest in scale: "can act most effectually" is a claim about *possibility and power*, which the rest of the chapter then argues into probability.

Darwin's own answer, given before the argument, is characteristically restrained: "I think we shall see that it can act most effectually."

# Variation, Plasticity, and Heredity

## Where we are in the argument

Chapter IV opens with two questions, not two claims:

> "How will the struggle for existence, discussed too briefly in the last chapter, act in regard to variation? Can the principle of selection, which we have seen is so potent in the hands of man, apply in nature?"

Darwin has already spent Chapter I on variation under domestication, Chapter II on variation under nature, and Chapter III on the struggle for existence. Now he wants to fuse them. But before he draws his conclusion, he asks the reader to hold four things in mind. They function as the **premises** of the argument, and if you accept all four the conclusion becomes very hard to resist. This lesson is about those premises — what each one asserts, what kind of evidence stands behind it, and why Darwin needs it.

Here is the passage, with the premises marked:

> "Let it be borne in mind **[1]** in what an endless number of strange peculiarities our domestic productions, and, **[2]** in a lesser degree, those under nature, vary; and **[3]** how strong the hereditary tendency is. **[4]** Under domestication, it may be truly said that the whole organisation becomes in some degree plastic."

(A fifth premise about the "infinitely complex and close-fitting" relations of organisms follows immediately; we treat it in the next lesson.)

## Premise 1: the endless strangeness of domestic variation

Notice Darwin's phrasing: not "how much" domestic productions vary, but *in what an endless number of strange peculiarities* they vary. Two distinct ideas are packed in.

- **Endless number** — variation is not confined to a few characters. It appears everywhere in the organism.
- **Strange peculiarities** — the variations are not the ones a designer would have predicted or a naturalist would have thought possible. They are odd, arbitrary, unforeseen.

Darwin's readers already knew the evidence. From the wild rock-pigeon, breeders had produced the pouter with its inflated crop, the fantail with its thirty-odd tail feathers, the short-faced tumbler with a beak like a finch's, birds differing in the number of vertebrae, in the width of the gape, in the length of the eyelid, in the behaviour of the young in the nest. From a single wild cabbage came the cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower and kohlrabi — a plant selected variously for its leaves, its stem, its flower buds. Nobody set out to discover that flower buds *could* be enlarged into a cauliflower; breeders found it out by seizing on peculiarities as they turned up.

That is the force of "strange." Variation is not a short list of options. It is a supply whose limits nobody has found.

## Premise 2: "in a lesser degree, those under nature"

This is the most easily skipped clause and one of the most important. Darwin's whole case is an argument from domestication to nature, and the analogy fails at once if wild organisms are essentially uniform — if variation is a peculiar disease of pampered, artificially fed, artificially bred stock.

So Darwin concedes and asserts in the same breath. He **concedes** that wild variation is less: domestic productions vary more freely, and Chapter I offers a reason — changed conditions of life, especially altered food and climate over generations, seem to loosen the reproductive system and make offspring more variable. He **asserts** that wild variation is nonetheless real. Chapter II is his evidence: the disputes among naturalists over whether a given form is a species or a variety, the many "doubtful species," the fact that large and widespread genera contain the most variable species. Where taxonomists argue, variation exists.

The concession costs him something, and he pays it. Nature has less raw material to work on than the breeder does. Darwin's answer, developed later in the chapter, is that nature compensates with vastly more time and a far more searching scrutiny.

> **A note on strategy.** "In a lesser degree" is characteristic Darwin. He states the objection to his own case before a critic can, and in doing so he earns the reader's trust for the claims he does not qualify.

## Premise 3: the strength of the hereditary tendency

A variation that is not inherited is useless to Darwin. If the offspring of a fast horse were no faster than average, breeding would be pointless and selection — natural or artificial — would have nothing to accumulate. Every breeder's practice presupposes heredity: you keep the best animals *for breeding*, and you do it because the peculiarity reappears in the young.

What is remarkable is that Darwin makes this premise carry so much weight while frankly not knowing how heredity works. He had no genes, no chromosomes, no particulate theory of inheritance. (His later attempt, "pangenesis," was wrong.) He treats heredity as a well-attested **fact of observation**, not as a mechanism he can explain — the same way an engineer may rely on gravity without a theory of gravitation.

This blind spot later cost him. Under the prevailing assumption of *blending* inheritance, a novel favourable variation would be halved in each generation of crossing and swamped before selection could act on it. The objection was pressed hard by Fleeming Jenkin in 1867, and Darwin never fully answered it. Mendelian, particulate inheritance — which does not blend or dilute — repaired the gap in the twentieth century. So Premise 3 is both the premise Darwin was most confident about and the one whose foundation he understood least.

## Premise 4: the whole organisation becomes plastic

> "Under domestication, it may be truly said that the whole organisation becomes in some degree plastic."

Read the sentence carefully; both qualifiers matter.

- **"the whole organisation"** — not just size or colour, the traits a casual observer notices, but the skeleton, the viscera, the instincts, the timing of development. There is no protected core that variation cannot reach. This is the crucial claim: if some parts were fixed, evolutionary change would have hard limits and the deep transformations Darwin needs would be impossible.
- **"in some degree"** — plasticity is a matter of degree, not an absence of constraint. Darwin is not claiming that anything whatever can be produced from anything.

Beware the word *plastic*. In modern biology, "phenotypic plasticity" means something Darwin does **not** mean here: the capacity of one genotype to produce different phenotypes in different environments (a water-buttercup growing different leaves above and below the water line). Darwin's plasticity is about the **heritable** malleability of a lineage under selection over generations — the organisation can be moulded into new stable forms and those forms breed true. A modern gloss would be something like: standing heritable variation exists in essentially every character, so selection can move essentially any character.

## The tension that makes the system work

Premises 1 and 3 pull in opposite directions, and Darwin needs both at full strength.

| Premise | What it supplies | What it would do alone |
|---|---|---|
| Variation / plasticity | Novelty; the raw material | Endless flux; nothing accumulates, offspring resemble nothing |
| Heredity | Fidelity; the ratchet | Perfect copies forever; no change is ever possible |

Evolution requires **imperfect** copying: transmission faithful enough that an advantage persists, unfaithful enough that new advantages appear. A useful test of whether you have understood the passage is whether you can see that these two premises are in tension, and why the tension is not a flaw in the argument but its engine.

## Worked example: tracing the premises through a single case

Take the greyhound.

1. **Variation (P1):** among dogs of a litter, some are marginally longer in the leg, deeper in the chest, lighter in the loin. Nobody arranged this; the peculiarities simply turn up.
2. **Lesser variation in nature (P2):** the same kinds of small differences exist among wolves — less conspicuously, but they are there.
3. **Heredity (P3):** the fastest bitch, bred, throws pups that are on average faster than the pups of a slow one. Without this, step 4 never begins.
4. **Plasticity (P4):** the breeder is not limited to leg length. Over generations the skull narrows, the heart enlarges, the temperament alters, the whole organisation shifts together. Nothing turned out to be off-limits.

Now substitute a hunting advantage for the breeder's preference and thousands of generations for a human lifetime, and you have the argument Darwin is about to make.

## What the premises do not yet establish

Be precise about the state of the argument at this point in the text. Established: variation exists, is widespread, is heritable, and reaches the whole organisation. **Not yet established:** that any of this variation is *useful* in nature, or that there is any agency to pick out the useful. Darwin has assembled the raw material and the mechanism of transmission. He has not yet supplied a selector. That is the work of the sentences that follow — the complexity of organic relations, the analogy from variations useful to man, and the superabundance of births.

## Reading exercise

Rewrite Darwin's premise sentence as four numbered propositions in plain modern English. Then, for each one, write a sentence beginning "If this were false, then…". You should find that falsifying any single premise breaks the argument at a different joint — which is a good sign that Darwin included no premise he did not need.

lessons.content:
# Complex and Close-Fitting Relations

## The sentence at the hinge of the argument

In the opening paragraph of Chapter IV, Darwin asks a question that the whole book depends on: can selection, so powerful in the hands of breeders, operate in nature? Before he answers, he asks his reader to hold three things in mind. The third is the one we study here:

> "Let it be borne in mind how infinitely complex and close-fitting are the mutual relations of all organic beings to each other and to their physical conditions of life."

This is not decoration. It is a premise doing hard logical work. Notice where it sits: between the observation that organisms vary heritably, and the conclusion that variations *useful in some way* must sometimes arise. Without the premise about relations, the conclusion would not follow.

## Why the premise is needed

A sceptic in 1859 might grant everything else and still balk. Yes, pigeons vary; yes, breeders can accumulate variation. But the breeder *wants* something — a shorter beak, a fatter fleece — and steers toward it. Nature wants nothing. So why should a random-seeming variation happen to be *useful*? Usefulness looks like it requires a purpose, and nature has none to supply.

Darwin's answer is that usefulness does not require a purpose; it requires only a relation. A variation is useful if it improves an organism's standing in some relation it already stands in. And organisms stand in an enormous number of such relations.

Unpack the phrase:

- **"Mutual relations of all organic beings to each other"** — predator to prey, parasite to host, plant to pollinator, seedling to the seedling beside it, bird to the insect it eats and to the hawk that eats it. These relations are *mutual*: each party is a condition of life for the other.
- **"And to their physical conditions of life"** — temperature, drought, soil, salinity, light.
- **"Infinitely complex"** — the relations are not a short list but a dense web, and they chain: changing one alters others.
- **"Close-fitting"** — the fit is tight. Small differences matter, because the margins on which survival turns are narrow.

Darwin had illustrated this in the previous chapter with the famous chain running from cats to field-mice to humble-bees to red clover: an increase in cats near a village raises the clover crop, because cats eat the mice that destroy the bees' combs, and only humble-bees fertilise red clover. The point of such examples is not their charm but their implication for variation.

## From complexity to conceivable usefulness

Here is the inference, laid out:

1. Each organism is embedded in a very large number of relations, biotic and physical.
2. Each relation is close-fitting — slight differences in an organism affect how it fares in that relation.
3. Therefore each relation is a separate *dimension along which a variation could be an improvement*.
4. Variation is copious and heritable, and thousands of generations are available.
5. Therefore it is not improbable that, now and then, a variation arises that helps in *some* one of these relations.

Step 3 is the crux. The complexity of relations multiplies the number of ways a change can pay. A slightly longer tongue, a slightly stickier seed coat, a slightly earlier flowering, a slightly duller feather, a slightly better tolerance of salt — none of these needs to be an all-round improvement in some abstract sense. It only needs to be an advantage in one of the countless close-fitting relations the creature is already caught in. "Useful" is not a property of the variation alone; it is a property of the variation *in a relational context*.

Compare Darwin's own analogy: variations useful to man have undoubtedly occurred. Man is only one further relation an organism might stand in, and a rather narrow one. If a single relation — to a human breeder with a particular taste — has produced greyhounds, carrier pigeons and merino sheep, how much more can be expected of the indefinitely many relations of nature?

## "The great and complex battle of life"

Darwin's phrase for the arena is deliberate. It is a *battle* (Chapter III's struggle for existence, waged not only against enemies but against drought, against competitors for the same square inch of ground) and it is *complex* — there is no single front. Because it is complex, there is no single measure of fitness and no single way to win. Two organisms of the same species may improve their prospects by opposite variations, if they are exploiting different relations. This idea will grow, later in the chapter, into the principle of Divergence of Character.

The complexity also cuts the other way, and Darwin says so in the same breath: "any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed." A tightly fitted system is easy to disturb. Close fit means that departures are usually for the worse — which is precisely why the rare departure for the better is worth preserving, and why selection is a sieve rather than a creative agent that anticipates needs.

## What Darwin is *not* claiming

Three common misreadings are worth blocking:

- **He is not claiming variations arise because they are needed.** The relations make usefulness *possible and occasionally realised*; they do not summon the variation. Variation is presented as given, from the domestic examples, and is not directed by the relation it happens to serve.
- **He is not claiming every variation matters.** He explicitly notes that "variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element" — his example being polymorphic species. Close-fitting relations make many variations consequential, not all of them.
- **He is not claiming the environment is only physical.** Nineteenth-century transmutationists often thought of climate and soil as the shaping forces. Darwin's stress on relations *to each other* moves the chief agency to other organisms — which is why his environment is never static: it is made of things that are themselves evolving.

## A worked illustration

Take a plant on a hillside. List its relations: to soil depth, to summer drought, to the grazing sheep, to the fungus in its roots, to the beetle that bores its stem, to the bee that carries its pollen, to the neighbouring grass shading its seedlings, to the finch that eats its seeds, to the frost date.

Now ask: how many distinct kinds of heritable change could be an advantage?

- Deeper roots (drought, soil)
- Bitterer leaves (sheep)
- Thicker stem tissue (beetle)
- Brighter or differently timed flowers (bee)
- Taller seedlings (grass)
- Harder seed coat (finch)
- Later bud-break (frost)

Seven relations, seven or more open avenues — and each avenue admits many degrees. Multiply this by thousands of generations and the initially odd-sounding claim, that a *useful* variation should sometimes turn up, stops sounding odd. That is the entire persuasive purpose of the "infinitely complex and close-fitting" clause.

## Summary

Darwin's premise about relations converts a suspicious-looking claim — that useless-seeming variability should sometimes throw up something useful — into an expected one. Complexity supplies many dimensions in which improvement is possible; close fit ensures that even slight differences register in those dimensions. Together they make "useful in some way to each being in the great and complex battle of life" a low bar rather than a miracle, and so clear the ground for natural selection: the preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious ones.

# Advantage, However Slight

## The passage at the heart of the theory

In Chapter IV of *On the Origin of Species*, Darwin arrives at the argument the whole book has been building toward. It is worth reading slowly, because it is not a description of nature so much as a **chain of inference** — a series of premises, each defended earlier in the book, that lock together into a conclusion.

> "Can it, then, be thought improbable, seeing that variations useful to man have undoubtedly occurred, that other variations useful in some way to each being in the great and complex battle of life, should sometimes occur in the course of thousands of generations? If such do occur, can we doubt (remembering that many more individuals are born than can possibly survive) that individuals having any advantage, however slight, over others, would have the best chance of surviving and of procreating their kind? On the other hand, we may feel sure that any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed. This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection."

Notice that Darwin does not report an experiment here. He asks two rhetorical questions and draws a conclusion. The force of the argument comes from the fact that each premise is, by this point, hard to deny.

## Unpacking the chain

**Premise 1 — Organisms vary, and variation is heritable.** Darwin has spent Chapters I and II establishing this. Under domestication "the whole organisation becomes in some degree plastic," and "how strong the hereditary tendency is." Variation under nature is smaller in degree, but real.

**Premise 2 — Some variations are useful.** This is the step Darwin defends by analogy. Breeders have *undoubtedly* found variations useful to human purposes — fatter sheep, faster pigeons, sweeter fruit. If variation throws up traits that happen to suit a pigeon fancier's arbitrary taste, why should it never throw up a trait that suits the organism's own needs? Given "how infinitely complex and close-fitting are the mutual relations of all organic beings to each other and to their physical conditions of life," there are countless dimensions along which a small change could matter.

**Premise 3 — Time is long.** Useful variations need not be common. They need only occur "sometimes... in the course of thousands of generations." Darwin deliberately lowers the bar: he asks the reader to concede only rarity, not abundance.

**Premise 4 — More individuals are born than can survive.** This is the Malthusian premise from Chapter III, the struggle for existence. Darwin flags it parenthetically, as something already agreed. It is what converts a difference in *quality* into a difference in *fate*: if every offspring survived, an advantage would change nothing about who leaves descendants.

**Conclusion — Individuals with any advantage, however slight, have the best chance of surviving and procreating their kind.** And symmetrically, injurious variations are "rigidly destroyed." Darwin names the two-sided process — preservation of the favourable, rejection of the injurious — *Natural Selection*.

## Why "however slight" is doing so much work

A reader in 1859 might grant that a monstrously well-equipped animal would out-survive a crippled one, and still doubt that this explains the origin of species. Darwin's phrase "any advantage, however slight" blocks that retreat. The argument does not require dramatic advantages. It requires only that:

- the advantage be real, and
- the surplus of births over survivors be large enough that even a small edge shifts the odds.

Selection is a statistical process. No individual is guaranteed anything; a slightly better-camouflaged moth can still be eaten by chance. Darwin's careful wording is **"best chance"**, not "certainty." But repeat the lottery across a large population and thousands of generations, and slight differences in odds accumulate into large differences in composition.

## The three-way sorting of variation

Darwin immediately adds a third category that is often forgotten:

> "Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic."

So variation is sorted three ways, not two:

| Type of variation | Fate under natural selection |
| --- | --- |
| Favourable | Preserved; tends to spread |
| Injurious | "Rigidly destroyed" |
| Neither useful nor injurious | Untouched; "a fluctuating element" |

That third row is a mark of Darwin's honesty and of the theory's precision. Natural selection is not a claim that *every* trait has a purpose. It explains adaptation; it explicitly declines to explain neutral variation, which is left free to fluctuate. (Modern biology calls such variation *neutral*, and a whole theory — the neutral theory of molecular evolution — grew up around it a century later. Darwin's word for its visible result was *polymorphic* species: species that persistently come in several forms.)

## A worked illustration

Suppose a beetle population produces 200 eggs per pair per season, but the population is stable — so on average only 2 of those 200 survive to breed. Ninety-nine percent are eliminated. Now imagine a variant with a shell pigment that makes it slightly harder to spot, raising its chance of surviving from 1.00% to 1.01%.

Nothing dramatic happens in one generation. Almost all the variants still die. But the *proportion* of variants among survivors ticks upward, every generation, without fail. This is precisely Darwin's structure: a huge surplus of births supplies the raw material of elimination; a slight advantage biases who is eliminated; heredity carries the bias forward; time compounds it.

Remove any one premise and the argument collapses:

- No heredity → the advantage dies with the individual.
- No surplus of births → nothing is eliminated, so no sorting occurs.
- No variation → nothing to sort.
- Little time → the compounding never becomes visible.

## Selection as a name, not a force

Darwin's last sentence in the passage is a definition: "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, **I call** Natural Selection." He is not introducing a new power in nature. He is giving a name to the *outcome* of premises the reader has already accepted. Nothing pushes organisms toward improvement; differential survival and reproduction is simply what necessarily happens when heritable variation meets a shortage of places in the next generation.

This is why the argument is so hard to resist. To reject the conclusion, you must deny one of the premises — that organisms vary heritably, that some variations help, or that more are born than can live.

## Points to carry forward

1. Darwin's core argument is deductive in shape: variation + heredity + occasional utility + overproduction ⇒ differential survival.
2. The magnitude of the advantage is irrelevant to the logic; only its reality and its heritability matter.
3. Selection is probabilistic ("best chance"), not guaranteed for any individual.
4. Natural selection has two active edges (preservation and rejection) and one blind spot (neutral variation).

lessons.title: Naming the Principle

# Naming the Principle

## The sentence itself

At the close of his opening argument in Chapter IV, Darwin does something a scientific writer does only rarely: he stops and christens a thing.

> "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection."

Everything before this sentence is an argument; everything after it is the working out of a named principle. It is worth slowing down here, because the definition is unusually compact and every clause is load-bearing.

## The two sides of the definition

Notice first that the definition has **two halves**, joined by "and":

1. **Preservation** of favourable variations
2. **Rejection** of injurious variations

Darwin builds up to these separately in the paragraph. The first half arrives as a rhetorical question:

> "can we doubt (remembering that many more individuals are born than can possibly survive) that individuals having any advantage, however slight, over others, would have the best chance of surviving and of procreating their kind?"

The second arrives as a flat assertion, in a noticeably harsher register:

> "On the other hand, we may feel sure that any variation in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed."

The asymmetry of tone is deliberate. Preservation is probabilistic — "the best chance" — because a favourable variation only *tends* to be kept; its bearer may still be crushed by a falling branch. Destruction of the injurious is stated as a near-certainty, "rigidly destroyed." Darwin needs both halves because either alone would be a weaker engine. Preservation alone would let harmful novelties accumulate alongside good ones; rejection alone would merely police the species back to its existing type, a conservative force with no power to build anything new. Together they form a **ratchet**: the good is kept, the bad is cleared away, and the population can only move in one direction over time.

## The third category: the neutral

Darwin immediately adds a limit clause, and this is the mark of a careful definition rather than a slogan:

> "Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic."

This is a striking piece of intellectual discipline. Having just named a principle he believes explains the whole organic world, Darwin's very next move is to say what it does *not* do. Neutral variation drifts. It is "a fluctuating element" — unpinned, free to wobble — and he points to polymorphic species (those with several stable forms coexisting) as possible evidence.

The clause matters for three reasons:

- **It makes the principle falsifiable in scope.** Natural selection is not a universal explanation of every trait; it is a filter that acts only where utility or injury is at stake.
- **It follows from the definition, rather than being tacked on.** If selection *is* preservation-of-the-useful plus rejection-of-the-injurious, then by simple logic something neither useful nor injurious falls through the mesh.
- **It anticipates a whole later science.** Twentieth-century population genetics would make neutral variation and genetic drift central. Darwin does not develop it, but he does not deny it either.

## The premises smuggled into the definition

The named principle only works because of things established earlier and carried into this paragraph as given:

| Premise | Where Darwin gestures at it | Work it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organisms vary | "an endless number of strange peculiarities" | Supplies the raw material |
| Variation is heritable | "how strong the hereditary tendency is" | Lets an advantage persist beyond one life |
| Overproduction of offspring | "many more individuals are born than can possibly survive" | Guarantees a filter must operate |
| Relations are complex and close-fitting | "infinitely complex and close-fitting are the mutual relations" | Makes it plausible that small differences matter |

Remove any one and the definition becomes inert. Without heredity, a favourable variation is preserved for a lifetime and then lost. Without overproduction, everything survives and nothing is rejected. The definition is the visible tip of a four-part argument.

## What work does the *name* do?

Darwin could have written "this process" and carried on. Instead he coined a term, and the choice repays scrutiny.

**"Selection" imports an analogy.** The whole preceding move of the book has been: breeders select, and they achieve extraordinary changes in pigeons, dogs, cabbages. Darwin asks directly, "Can the principle of selection, which we have seen is so potent in the hands of man, apply in nature?" By naming his principle *selection*, he lends it the borrowed credibility of something his readers already accept and can watch happening in a farmyard. The name is a compressed argument.

**"Natural" does the disanalogising.** It marks the crucial difference: there is no selector. The adjective says *this operates without intention, in the ordinary course of nature*. It also carries a contrast to "artificial" — the domestic case is the special, contrived one; Darwin's is the general case.

**The costs of the metaphor.** The name has been argued over ever since. "Selection" suggests an agent choosing, and Darwin was accused of covertly reintroducing a designer; he spent later editions insisting the word was metaphorical, in the same way chemists speak of elements having "affinities." Alfred Russel Wallace urged him to adopt Herbert Spencer's phrase "survival of the fittest" instead, which Darwin partly did in later editions — though that phrase brought problems of its own, being nearly circular and emphasising survival over reproduction, when Darwin's own wording is careful to say "surviving *and of procreating their kind*."

Note too that the name is one-sided in a way the definition is not. "Selection" evokes the picking-out, the preservation; it does not evoke the rigid destruction. The negative half of the process hides inside a positive-sounding word.

## A worked reading

Try applying the definition strictly to a case.

*Suppose a beetle population contains individuals with slightly thicker wing-cases.*

- If thicker cases reduce desiccation in a dry season, and more offspring are born than can survive, thick-cased beetles have "the best chance of surviving and of procreating their kind." **Preservation.**
- If the thickness costs so much in flight that predators take those beetles first, the variation is "in the least degree injurious" and is "rigidly destroyed." **Rejection.**
- If the thickness makes no difference whatever to the beetle's life in its actual conditions, natural selection does nothing at all. The trait becomes "a fluctuating element" and may drift to any frequency.

The key discipline here is that *favourable* and *injurious* are not properties of the variation in the abstract. They are relations between the variation and the "infinitely complex and close-fitting" conditions of life. Change the conditions and the same trait switches category. Darwin's definition contains no list of good traits — only a rule about consequences.

## Summary

Darwin's naming sentence packs a two-sided filter into a single clause, explicitly exempts the neutral, and borrows a term from animal breeding whose analogical force he then qualifies with the word "natural." The name is doing rhetorical work — recruiting a familiar, visible process to vouch for an invisible one — and it is doing conceptual work, insisting that the process is impersonal. Its one weakness is that it names only the preserving half of a principle that depends equally on destruction.

lessons.title: The Neutral Case and Polymorphic Species
lessons.content:
# The Neutral Case and Polymorphic Species

## A sentence easy to skip past

At the close of his first definition of natural selection, Darwin adds a short qualification that is easy to read straight through:

> "This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection. **Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic.**"

The first sentence is the famous one. The second is the one that shows Darwin thinking carefully about the *limits* of his own principle. Having just argued that any advantage "however slight" gives a better chance of surviving, and that anything "in the least degree injurious would be rigidly destroyed," he immediately marks out a third category: variations that do neither.

## The three-way logic

Darwin's argument in this passage is a simple exhaustive division of variation by its effect on the bearer's chance of surviving and reproducing:

| Effect of the variation | Fate under natural selection |
|---|---|
| Useful, however slightly | Preserved — the bearer has "the best chance of surviving and of procreating their kind" |
| Injurious, in the least degree | "Rigidly destroyed" |
| Neither useful nor injurious | **Not affected at all** — "left a fluctuating element" |

Notice that the third row is not an exception grudgingly admitted. It follows *necessarily* from how Darwin has defined the mechanism. Natural selection is not a force that shapes everything in an organism; it is the differential survival of individuals caused by differences that matter to survival. If a difference does not matter to survival, there is nothing for selection to grip. Selection has no separate power to tidy up, standardise, or perfect a character; it acts only through the deaths and reproductive successes it causes.

This is why the passage is a genuine strength of the theory rather than a weakness. A principle that explained *every* feature of *every* organism would be unfalsifiable and, in Darwin's own terms, useless. By specifying what natural selection cannot do, Darwin makes it a real causal claim.

## "A fluctuating element"

The phrase is worth dwelling on. Darwin does not say a neutral variation would be *fixed*, or *lost*, or held at some stable value. He says it would be *fluctuating* — free to drift up and down in frequency, with no directing hand. Two individuals of the same species might differ in such a character with no consequence whatever; the population might show a scatter of forms with no one form displacing the others.

So neutral variation is not predicted to disappear. It is predicted to be *unruly*. Where a character is under selection, we expect the species to converge on a form suited to its conditions; where it is not, we expect the variability itself to persist and wander.

## Polymorphic species as the visible evidence

Darwin then reaches for an observation: "as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic." A **polymorphic species**, in the naturalists' usage he is invoking, is one that appears in several distinct forms at once — variable in some character to a degree that frustrated the classifiers of his day, who could not decide whether they were looking at varieties, races, or separate species at all.

His suggestion is that these puzzling cases may be exactly what neutral variation looks like from the outside. If a set of characters is indifferent to the organism's welfare, selection will not have pruned the variation away, and the species will present the naturalist with a confusing bouquet of forms rather than one well-defined type. The theory therefore does more than tolerate polymorphism; it offers a reason for it.

A worked illustration of the reasoning:

- Suppose two land snails differ in the exact banding pattern on their shells.
- If banding affects how visible a snail is to a thrush, the difference is not neutral: birds will do the selecting, and one pattern will come to predominate in that habitat.
- If, in some other habitat, banding makes no difference to predation, temperature, mating, or anything else, then no snail dies for its banding. Both patterns persist; new ones may appear and linger. The species looks polymorphic.

The key move is that neutrality is not a property of a character in the abstract. It is a property of a character *in a particular set of conditions of life*. Darwin has already insisted that "infinitely complex and close-fitting are the mutual relations of all organic beings to each other and to their physical conditions of life" — which means a character indifferent today may become useful or injurious when circumstances shift.

## Darwin's hedge: "perhaps"

Darwin writes "as **perhaps** we see." He is not claiming to have demonstrated that polymorphic characters are neutral. He is offering a candidate class of observations that the neutral case would predict, while leaving open that some of these forms may turn out to be under selection after all — maintained by causes not yet understood.

This cautious phrasing is characteristic and instructive. The logical claim (neutral variations are untouched by selection) is certain, because it follows from the definition. The empirical claim (polymorphic species show us such variations) is offered tentatively, because it depends on facts he cannot yet establish.

## Why this matters for the rest of the argument

Three consequences follow for anyone reading further into the *Origin*:

1. **Not every trait needs an adaptive story.** When we later meet characters of "trifling importance," we should not assume automatically that selection made them; Darwin has left room for other explanations.
2. **Variation is the raw material, not the product.** Selection sorts variation, it does not generate it. Where sorting is absent, the raw variability shows through undisguised.
3. **The theory makes differential predictions.** Characters that matter should be relatively uniform within a population and fitted to conditions; characters that do not should be variable. That contrast is testable — and it is exactly the contrast Darwin invokes with polymorphic species.

## Summary

Darwin's definition of natural selection has two active clauses (preserve the favourable, reject the injurious) and one silent clause (do nothing to the indifferent). The silent clause predicts that neutral characters will remain a "fluctuating element" in a species, and Darwin tentatively identifies polymorphic species — those exasperatingly variable forms — as the place where such fluctuation may be visible.
